items.headline: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
items.blurb: Ukraine says the missile and drone attack on the strategic bridge in the Russian-annexed Crimea took weeks to plan.
items.text: Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort. Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight. Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good. While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin. items.blurb: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and…
items.text: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”. items.headline: How the attack on Crimean Bridge unfolded
items.blurb: One of the key symbols of Russia's occupation of Ukraine has suffered major damage after a seven-stage attack by Kyiv.
items.text: Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula. A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before". But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures. The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday. For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. items.headline: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
items.blurb: The US-led board has decried continued fighting in Gaza and delays in implementing the terms of a 2025 ceasefire deal.
items.text: The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza. In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse. “The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained. The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza. Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. items.headline: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
items.blurb: Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
items.text: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country. Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates. The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device. Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison. A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League.

items.headline: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
items.blurb: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
items.text: Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it is not reinstating ousted founder Jensen Huang. In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Collette Kress said Nvidia's "roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater". The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company recovering some recent losses in after-hours trading. Earlier on Tuesday Huang, said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a possible spy for China. "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones told investors on Tuesday. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period. Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13%

items.headline: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
items.blurb: Crew say their boat was attacked by drones launched from US-operated vessel as part of 'manifestly unlawful' campaign.
items.text: A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March. The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just. It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador. “We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.” The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months. items.text: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. items.headline: Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
items.blurb: Markle is being held in custody in the US after one charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.
items.text: Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material. The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC. Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material. Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment. Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM child sexual abuse and exploitation material, and one count of possession of CSAEM material". Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country. items.blurb: The move follows a full court meeting in which the CJI made told judges that they must adjudicate matters strictly in accordance with their rosters.
items.text: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , in consultation with the four most senior judges of the Supreme Court, has shifted at least two matters away from a bench headed by justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah over its decision to expand individual disputes into nationwide public interest litigations (PILs), according to people aware of the matter. The decision marks an unusual institutional intervention to enforce strict adherence to the roster and comes after the CJI made it clear at a full court meeting last month that judges cannot assume jurisdiction over subjects not assigned to them. The two matters involve a nationwide examination of regulatory failures in private universities and a separate exercise to address unauthorised constructions and misuse of residential properties across the country. Both had begun as individual disputes before justice Amanullah, whose roster does not include PILs but who expanded their scope to address wider systemic issues. items.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is developing artificial intelligence tools specifically designed for auditing, with projects ready for a pan-India rollout, CAG K Sanjay Murthy said on Tuesday. The country’s top auditor said that the access to digital systems allows audit teams to “examine full sets of transactions, and that analysis of data ahead of fieldwork guides field enquiries and has shortened the audit cycle”. The move was highlighted by Murthy at the conclusion of two-day Audit Diwas program in Delhi. “..access to the digital systems allow audit teams to examine full sets of transactions, and that analysis of data ahead of fieldwork guides field enquiries and has shortened the audit cycle. The department is building audit-specific AI rather than relying on general AI tools alone, and the projects (are) ready for pan-India rollout,” Murthy said. items.headline: Indian Army reverses dress-code change for senior officers; berets, shoulder titles to make a comeback
items.blurb: The revised order restores distinctive gears, including Gorkha Rifles hats, maroon berets for Special Forces and black berets for armoured regiments.
items.text: Generals from the Gorkha Rifles can once again wear their trademark hats, Special Forces brass can return to their iconic maroon berets, and senior officers of armoured regiments can don black berets, as the Indian Army has rolled back dress code changes introduced three years ago, according to an internal communique. In 2023, the army ordered a new, common uniform for officers of brigadier rank and above to bolster a common identity and approach in service matters among the senior leadership. The directive was rescinded in a November 13 letter titled “Dress for Brig & Above Rk Offrs”, seen by HT. The decision to switch to the common uniform was taken in April 2023 during the Army Commanders’ Conference, chaired by then Army chief General Manoj Pande, and implemented in August that year. The changes stipulated that senior officers would no longer wear accoutrements specific to their respective arms and services; the ubiquitous shoulder lanyard was also abolished; and officers were required to wear dark green berets, a standardised belt and brass rank insignia. The results come amid a leadership transition after CEO Jensen Huang resigned on 12 November. The company posted revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended 25 October 2026, up 20% from $96.2 billion in the previous quarter and compared with $57 billion in the year-ago period. Here are the key takeaways from Nvidia, a global leader in AI and accelerated computing, on its Q3 fiscal 2027 results. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter ended 25 October 2026, up 103% year on year and 20% from the previous quarter. Data Centre revenue reached a record $107.6 billion, up 110% year on year. Edge Computing revenue also grew 42% to $8.2 billion. Nvidia expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. Its forecast excludes data centre compute revenue from China. Longtime CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. items.headline: End of the road for Jensen Huang? Nvidia Board Chairman Harvey Jones says no intention to rehire him as CEO
items.blurb: Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO. The company has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent leader, while interim CEO Colette Kress oversees operations during an investigation into Huang’s departure.
items.text: Nvidia board Chairman Harvey Jones has clarified that the company does not intend to rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, amid growing calls for his return. Jones made the remarks as he opened the conference call with investors on Tuesday to announce Nvidia’s Q3 results . “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” he said. Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO. "We want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person," he added. Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said the board unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him. Huang has said he would return if the board decided it was in the company’s best interests. Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. The board has hired Heidrick & Struggles to help find a permanent successor.

Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. items.headline: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
items.blurb: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t.
items.text: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. items.blurb: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.
items.text: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. items.headline: Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic after its IPO
items.blurb: Amazon will own just under 15% of Anthropic after the IPO, with the option to go much higher. Google is a close second with holdings of nearly 14%.
items.text: Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google. While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact). Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the day when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity. These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. items.headline: Perplexity May Launch IPO As Early As Q1 CY27: CEO Aravind Srinivas
items.blurb: AI major Perplexity has preponed its proposed IPO timeline and could file its draft IPO papers for a listing in…
items.text: Perplexity may file for an IPO as early as Q1 CY27, with CEO Aravind Srinivas saying its ARR has crossed $1 Bn. The accelerated IPO timeline has put Perplexity on course to potentially join OpenAI and Anthropic in the public markets. Perplexity's growth has been supported by its India push, which became the startup’s biggest market following strategic partnership with enterprise players. AI major Perplexity has preponed its proposed IPO timeline and could file its draft IPO papers for a listing in the US as early as Q1 2027. Speaking with CNBC, founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas revealed that Perplexity has managed to grow faster than expected which pushed the decision to fast-track the listing. “The rate at which our business is growing, I wouldn’t rule out filing something in the first quarter of 2027,” Srinivas said during the broadcast. As per him, the company has already touched an ARR (annual recurring revenue) of $1 Bn, surpassing its $750 Mn ARR expectations ahead of the IPO. items.headline: AI adoption, weak demand to keep India's IT services revenue growth subdued in FY27: Report
items.blurb: India's IT services sector may continue to face subdued revenue growth in the remaining months of FY27 as rising adoption of artificial intelligence shifts technology spending towards AI-focused companies and reduces demand for traditional services, according to a report by ICICI Securities.
